claims.text: Increasing Zr content in NbTiAlZr-based refractory high-entropy alloys enhances solid-solution strengthening.
Increasing Zr content reduces precipitation of brittle intergranular phases.
The proposed Zr increase improves high-temperature strength and ductility.
The proposed Zr increase improves mechanical behavior under irradiation without compromising thermal stability.
The baseline NbTiAlZr-based alloy containing about 5 at% Zr has a primarily B2 matrix.
Appreciable Laves-phase formation occurs at grain boundaries in the approximately 5 at% Zr baseline alloy.
The intervention is to increase Zr from approximately 5 at% to approximately 10 at% during powder synthesis and spark-plasma sintering.
The predicted benefits should hold at 1023–1123 K.
The predicted benefits should hold under Fe-ion implantation at fluences on the order of 10^15–10^16 ions/cm2.
Increasing Zr to approximately 10 at% will retain a B2 matrix.
Increasing Zr to approximately 10 at% will lower the volume fraction of deleterious grain-boundary Laves phases.
Increased Zr reduces the driving force for Laves-phase nucleation.
Reduced Laves-phase nucleation minimizes brittle precipitation at grain boundaries.
Microstructural control through Zr enrichment preserves thermal and irradiation stability.
Relative to the approximately 5 at% Zr baseline, the approximately 10 at% Zr alloy will have higher room-temperature yield strength and ductility.
Relative to the approximately 5 at% Zr baseline, the approximately 10 at% Zr alloy will have higher elevated-temperature yield strength and ductility.
The Zr-enriched alloy will exhibit less grain-boundary embrittlement under irradiation than the baseline.
Increasing Zr significantly beyond 10 at% could promote unwanted oxide formation.
Increasing Zr significantly beyond 10 at% could cause grain coarsening that negates the mechanical improvements.
Interactions between Zr and the other alloying elements could produce unexpected phase transformations.
